what is owed to you. Cephalus, in an easygoing

or someone who was in a very depressed"--we might say a

How do you explain that? Would you do that if justice
means paying your debts and giving back to each what is
owed?" At that moment,
Cephalus excuses himself from the dialogue and says,
rather abruptly, "I have to go out and continue
my sacrifices in the garden." Socrates, in other words,
has broken the bond of tradition and traditional
authority that holds the ancient city and the ancient family
together. Cephalus is banished from the
dialogue. Tradition is banished and we
never hear another word about it for the next 400 or so pages.
That's the way Socrates begins this dialogue,
or that's the way Plato has Socrates begin it.
